content: Individuals in healthcare settings should be screened for tuberculosis (TB) during every interaction with the healthcare system. This includes routine visits such as vaccination days, maternal health appointments, nutritional screenings, and food support program visits. Due to the high risk of progression to active TB disease and the associated high mortality rate, symptom-based screening should also be conducted at every healthcare encounter. However, the combined symptom screening has low specificity, which may result in a significant number of false-positive cases, necessitating further diagnostic testing. Despite this, the benefits of TB treatment generally outweigh the risks of over-investigation and treatment, particularly given the high mortality associated with untreated TB in children living with HIV. Healthcare workers (HCWs) must closely monitor TB preventive therapy (TPT) or TB treatment and remain vigilant for alternative diagnoses. Determining whether a child has had close contact with a person with TB can be challenging. A thorough history of known exposures involving the parent, caregiver, and child is essential. While household contacts are often considered, in high TB incidence areas, close contact can occur in various community settings, such as schools, daycare centers, and religious gatherings. A study in South Africa revealed that only half of children with TB had a known household contact with a person with TB, and even young children were at significant risk of community-acquired TB infection outside the household. A high index of suspicion for TB should be maintained in young children, especially those living with HIV or with unknown HIV status in high TB incidence settings. Systematic screening for TB disease should be conducted among adolescents living with HIV using the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS). Adolescents reporting any of the following symptoms—current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats—should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. Additional screening methods for adolescents living with HIV may include C-reactive protein (CRP) testing (using a cut-off of >5 mg/L), chest X-rays (CXR), or molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs). Adolescents living with HIV who are inpatients in medical wards with a high TB prevalence (over 10%) should undergo systematic TB disease testing using mWRDs. Children and adolescents exposed to individuals with infectious TB are at high risk of developing TB disease. Contact investigation is crucial to identify exposed children and screen them for TB disease. This process requires dedicated human and financial resources and is most effective when conducted actively at the community or household level. Screening approaches differ slightly for children who are close contacts of a person with TB versus children living with HIV. For close contacts, screening tools include symptom screening (e.g., cough lasting more than two weeks, fever lasting more than two weeks, and poor weight gain or weight loss in the past three months) and/or CXR. For children living with HIV, symptom screening should include current cough, fever, poor weight gain in the past three months, or close contact with a person with TB. Screening should occur during every encounter with a healthcare worker. BCG vaccination is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis. It has demonstrated significant effectiveness, particularly in preventing severe forms of TB such as TB meningitis (TBM) and miliary TB when administered during the neonatal period. However, its protection against all forms of TB across all age groups is inconsistent. BCG also provides protection against leprosy and Buruli ulcer. Neonatal vaccination primarily prevents progression to disseminated TB forms. A systematic review found that BCG-vaccinated children exposed to infectious TB had a 19% lower risk of TB infection compared to unvaccinated children. BCG may also have nonspecific beneficial effects on all-cause mortality. BCG vaccination is recommended in countries or settings with high TB or leprosy incidence and areas where Buruli ulcer occurs. A single dose should be administered to all healthy neonates at birth. If not given at birth, it should be administered as soon as possible thereafter. In low TB incidence countries, selective vaccination of high-risk neonates may be considered. High-risk neonates include those living in households with individuals from high TB incidence countries, those traveling to or living in high TB incidence areas, or those with close contact with a person known to have TB. Revaccination is not recommended, even if tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results are negative. Children living with HIV should not receive BCG vaccination due to the increased risk of disseminated BCG disease. However, if they are on antiretroviral therapy (ART), clinically well, and immunologically stable (CD4% >25% for children under five years or CD4 count ≥200/mm³ for children over five years), they may be vaccinated. In settings without access to CD4 testing, immunological stability can be assessed clinically based on the absence of new opportunistic infections or symptoms. Neonates born to women with unknown HIV status should receive BCG vaccination. Neonates with unknown HIV status born to women living with HIV should also be vaccinated if they show no clinical evidence of HIV infection, regardless of the mother’s ART status. Adverse reactions to BCG vaccination are generally mild and include injection site reactions such as a papule that may progress to an ulcer and heal within 2–5 months, leaving a superficial scar. Regional lymph node swelling may also occur. Severe adverse events, though rare, include local abscesses, keloids, and disseminated BCG disease, which is associated with a high case fatality rate in infants living with HIV. Disseminated BCG disease can only be confirmed through positive mycobacterial culture with species identification.
